records.name_note: NC State: "Previously known as: Salvia brasiliensis" — an older synonym now superseded by Salvia splendens, the name used consistently by every cited source. RHS separately lists the cultivar 'Scarlet Sage' record's own "Name Status" as "Synonym," but this appears to be a database status for that specific cultivar entry (the same page's "Synonyms" field just repeats "Salvia splendens 'Scarlet Sage'"), not a proposal of a different accepted species name — no cited source uses any species binomial other than Salvia splendens, so this was not treated as a name conflict and scientific_name_accepted was kept equal to scientific_name_given. Common names vary: NC State/MOBOT/RHS/UGA use "Scarlet Sage" (RHS also lists "bonfire flower, firecrackers, globe of fire"); NC State also lists plain "Salvia"; Clemson calls it "Bedding Sage." Note that "scarlet sage" is also the common name UF/IFAS uses for the different species Salvia coccinea — the UGA source used here explicitly ties its "scarlet sage" text to the binomial Salvia splendens, so the common-name/species pairing was cross-checked before use.

water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_growing_days_est/water_dormant_days_est/water_estimate_basis: no source gives a watering-depth check method or a day-interval estimate for this outdoor bedding annual.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_active_months/fertilize_strength: Clemson and UGA recommend a slow-release fertilizer at planting (UGA adds a light feeding about a month later), but neither gives an ongoing interval in days or specific calendar months.
cool_rest_note: no source discusses a cool dormancy/rest period for this warm-season annual/tender perennial.

water_regime — removed on audit: The record asserts "keep_moist" citing only MOBOT's prose ("evenly moist, well-drained soils") and RHS's prose ("moist but well-drained... water in dry weather"). But MOBOT's own page has a separate STRUCTURED field, sitting directly above the quoted prose paragraph, reading `Water: Medium` (verified in raw HTML: div id=WaterRow -> "Water: Medium") — a categorical rating that contradicts the elevated "keep moist" claim drawn only from the adjacent prose. This is exactly the subtler defect pattern the audit brief flags: a cited source's own structured field contradicts the prose quote actually used. Additionally, two other sources already cited elsewhere in this same record for this species independently point away from a constant-moisture regime: Clemson's factsheet (used in this record for outdoor_sun_exposure and fertilizing) states, in its only growing-guidance section (there is no separate section for annual salvias, so this guidance covers them) — "Once established, most salvia species are quite drought-tolerant and require little care" and "Excessive water and fertilizer can increase fungal disease problems for salvias" — and UGA's article (used in this record for soil drainage) recommends "Water deeply, once a week, particularly during long, dry periods," a moderate/infrequent-deep-watering pattern, not an evenly-moist one. With a genuine, source-documented conflict on this harm-capable field, water_regime should have been left null rather than set to keep_moist.

records.name_note: Lathyrus odoratus is itself the currently accepted name, not a synonym: RHS's own name-status field reads "Name Status Correct," and NC State lists only older names (Lathyrus cyprius, L. maccaguenii, L. odoratus-zeylanicus) as "Previously known as" — i.e. synonyms of this species, not the reverse. No admissible source proposed a different accepted binomial, so there is no conflict to null out. Note for disambiguation only: NC State separately profiles a different species also commonly called "sweet pea" — Lathyrus latifolius (perennial/everlasting pea) — which is NOT this record; this record covers only the annual Lathyrus odoratus.

toxic_to_pets/toxicity_detail were deliberately sourced only from RHS's separate 'Pets:' tag ('Pods and seeds are not edible'); the fuller Lathyrism/paralysis symptom write-up on NC State and Missouri Botanical Garden is explicitly framed on those pages as toxicity 'to Humans', and that human-specific detail was withheld from the pet-facing fields to avoid blending targets.

toxicity_detail — removed on audit: The value embeds the human-specific Lathyrism mechanism/symptom list ('paralysis, slow and weak pulse, shallow breathing, convulsions') sourced from NC State's 'Poisonous to Humans' block and MoBOT's human-toxicity prose, directly inside the pet-facing toxicity_detail string -- the exact anti-pattern audit check #3 targets (mechanism/symptom content copied from a human-toxicity section into a pet-tagged field). The record's own text claims this human write-up 'was NOT carried into this pet-facing field,' but the symptom list is literally present in the field value, just wrapped in a disclaiming sentence. The only genuinely pet-specific admissible source (RHS's 'Pets:' tag) says nothing more than 'Pods and seeds are not edible' -- no mechanism, no symptoms. Failure scenario: a downstream consumer (e.g. a pet-safety UI) surfaces toxicity_detail verbatim to a worried pet owner, who reads 'paralysis... convulsions' inside the pet toxicity field and reasonably concludes these are the symptoms sweet pea causes in animals, when no admissible source makes that claim for pets at all. The field should state only what RHS's pet-specific tag supports ('pods and seeds are not edible') and omit the human symptom list rather than quoting-then-disclaiming it.

water_regime — removed on audit: Value 'dry_surface_between' rests only on a UF/IFAS quote ('reduce irrigation frequency once established... avoid over-irrigation') that never says to let the soil surface dry between waterings -- that specific category isn't literally in the quote. Worse, Missouri Botanical Garden's own plant page (cited elsewhere in this same record) has a structured field reading 'Water: Medium' and Culture text saying 'Needs regular moisture, but avoid overhead watering,' directly contradicting a dry-down regime. This is a harm-capable field where admissible sources genuinely disagree, and the record picked one value instead of surfacing the conflict or going null.

humidity_need — removed on audit: The cited UGA B1219 passage ('requires dry leaves and flowers to stay disease free... air movement that allows leaves to dry is crucial') is a foliar-disease-avoidance instruction about leaf-surface wetness, not a stated ambient relative-humidity preference. The same source document states elsewhere that vinca is commercially 'grown under warm, often humid conditions' and that the mitigation is airflow to dry foliage, not low ambient humidity -- i.e. the source's own content undercuts the blanket 'low' categorization the record derived from it.

records.name_note: RHS lists "Zinnia elegans" with Name Status "Correct" and gives "Zinnia violacea" as a synonym -- i.e. Zinnia elegans is the currently accepted name at RHS, not the other way round. NC State Extension and Missouri Botanical Garden both use "Zinnia elegans" as the current name throughout and do not flag it as superseded or list violacea at all, so all three admissible sources agree; no unresolved dispute over the accepted name was found.
unknowns: chill_damage_f: no admissible source gives a frost/cold damage-onset temperature; RHS's H2 hardiness rating (survives to 1-5°C but not freezing) is a mature-plant survival/tolerance floor, not a damage-onset threshold, so it was not used per the field definition.
day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no admissible source gives species-specific day or night ambient temperature ranges (only vague qualitative statements like 'thrive in the heat').
direct_sun_hours_max/light_fc_min/light_fc_good: outdoor sources describe sun exposure only as the 'full sun' duration category (6+ hours minimum), never as a footcandle value or an hours maximum.

humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: no source states a humidity need or percentage; sources only note that high humidity or wet foliage raises fungal leaf-spot risk, which is a disease-risk note, not a humidity requirement.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: NC State states the plant 'is not picky about soil pH' and lists acid, neutral, and alkaline as all tolerated -- that describes full-range tolerance, not a bounded preference range, so no numeric min/max was taken.

fertilize_active_months/fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength: Clemson's factsheet says only that 'a soil test is recommended before fertilizing,' with no schedule, month range, or strength given by any admissible source.
cool_rest_note/water_dormant_days_est: no admissible source discusses a dormancy or rest period for this annual species.

water_regime/water_growing_days_est/water_check_depth_cm/water_dry_down_target/water_estimate_basis: sources give non-equivalent water descriptors that don't resolve to one schema category -- NC State and Penn State tag it 'drought tolerant,' Clemson recommends about 1 inch/week watered at the base, Missouri Botanical Garden's structured field says 'Water: Medium,' and UGA says it needs 'ample moisture to thrive' -- so left null rather than guessed.
toxicity_detail: NC State's toxicity information is a bare non-toxic tag (cats/dogs/horses) with no mechanism or symptom text to quote, so no detail was taken.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: The record sets soil_drainage="fast" citing MOBOT's quote "Easily grown in humusy, evenly moist, well-drained soils in full sun." (verbatim-confirmed by direct fetch of plantfinder.mobot.org). That quote pairs 'well-drained' with 'evenly moist' -- language that does not cleanly resolve to the catalog's 'fast' drainage tier. MOBOT's own structured field on the same page (also verbatim-confirmed) reads "Water: Medium", reinforcing a moderate/moisture-retentive read rather than fast-draining. No admissible source ever uses the literal words fast/moderate/moisture_retentive for this species, so 'fast' is the record's own translation of ambiguous, moisture-qualified language -- exactly the situation this same catalog's other verified records (e.g. app/data/verified/b14-annual-flowers2.json, the water_regime/soil_drainage unknowns entries) treat by leaving soil_drainage null when 'well-drained' is paired with 'moist' rather than standing alone. The record should have left soil_drainage null (as it correctly did for water_regime, citing the same kind of cross-source moisture ambiguity) instead of asserting 'fast'.

scientific_name_accepted — removed on audit: The citation's claim label asserts 'Achillea millefolium (no synonym or name change indicated)', but the quoted MBG text ('Achillea millefolium, commonly called common yarrow, is a rhizomatous, spreading, upright to mat-forming perennial...') never addresses synonymy or taxonomic status at all -- it is simply a descriptive sentence that happens to use the name. Per audit criterion 1 ('does the quote ACTUALLY state this value, or does it merely sound related'), the quote does not establish the negative claim ('no synonym or name change indicated') the record attached to it; that portion of the claim has zero textual support in its own cited source. (Independently fetching MBG, NC State, and Clemson confirmed none of them flag a synonym for this species, and the RHS page -- found via search since the URL implied elsewhere in the record 404s -- lists Achillea millefolium as 'Name Status: Correct', so the underlying value is likely right, but the record's own citation does not demonstrate this.)

name_note — removed on audit: name_note claims 'All four admissible sources (NC State Extension, Clemson HGIC, Missouri Botanical Garden Plant Finder, and RHS) consistently use "Achillea millefolium"... none flag it as a synonym or note a taxonomic revision.' But the citations array contains zero citations for RHS, and zero citations establishing NC State's or Clemson's name/synonym status specifically (only one MBG citation exists for scientific_name_accepted, and per the finding above even that citation doesn't address synonymy). RHS is invoked here, and again in the unknowns entry for chill_damage_f ('RHS rating H7, "hardy in the severest European continental climates <-20C"'), with no citation URL anywhere in the record backing either mention -- the only RHS URL pattern implied by the record (rhs.org.uk/plants/achillea-millefolium/details) returns a 404; the real RHS page is at a different, numeric-ID URL the record never cites. The record asserts a four-source consensus its own evidence trail cannot substantiate.

water_regime, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_estimate_basis, water_check_depth_cm, water_dry_down_target: sources genuinely disagree on drought/moisture characterization at the species level — NC State calls it 'moderately resistant to...drought' while stressing 'moist, well-drained soil'; Missouri Botanical Garden rates water need 'Medium' and says it's 'Best in moist, organically rich soils'; UF/IFAS's structured Culture field rates 'Drought tolerance: high'; UMD gives only 'Moist to dry.' No single water_regime category can be chosen without favoring one source over another, so left null per the harm-capable-field rule.

soil_ph_min, soil_ph_max: UMD Extension states explicitly 'Soil texture and pH preferences, if any, are unknown'; NC State lists only broad categorical tags (acid <6.0, neutral 6.0-8.0, alkaline >8.0) spanning virtually the whole pH scale, which is not a usable numeric bound.
humidity_need, humidity_pct_min, humidity_pct_max: no admissible source discusses ambient humidity for this outdoor garden species.

light_fc_min, light_fc_good, direct_sun_hours_max: sources give only a duration category (full sun = 6+ hours; part shade = 2-6 hours), never a footcandle intensity or a stated upper-bound hour limit.

fertilize_interval_days, fertilize_active_months, fertilize_strength: NC State gives only qualitative guidance ('moderate fertility...avoid excess nitrogen'); RHS's specific fertilizing instructions (amount, product, season) are given for the Rudbeckia genus generally, not stated as R. hirta-specific, and don't specify a repeat interval.

toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail: none of the eight admissible sources checked, including targeted searches of Clemson's and UMD's pet-safe-plant material, address toxicity of Rudbeckia hirta to pets or to humans.

is_houseplant set false: no admissible source describes long-term indoor growing of the species; the container mentions found (Clemson's 'Toto' cultivars, RHS's 'Toto', Penn State's 'Autumn Colors'/'Cherry Brandy') are all for outdoor patio/garden containers, not indoor houseplant use.

name_note — removed on audit: name_note asserts that all eight admissible sources were checked and 'use "Rudbeckia hirta" consistently with no synonym or proposed name change flagged anywhere.' This is contradicted by the record's own cited UMD Extension page (used for citations 12 and 13, extension.umd.edu/resource/black-eyed-susan), which I fetched directly: it explicitly states that Maryland's R. hirta populations 'used to be classified as R. serotina, R. monticola, and R. brittonii' -- i.e. it does flag former synonyms, directly within a source the record itself relied on. Separately, 3 of the 8 sources the note claims were 'checked' (Clemson, Penn State, UGA) never appear anywhere in the citations array, so the sweeping 'checked ... no synonym flagged anywhere' claim is partly undocumented and, where it could be verified, is simply false. (The final scientific_name_accepted value of 'Rudbeckia hirta' itself still appears correct -- this is a soundness problem with the note's overclaimed certainty, per structural check #2, not with the chosen name.)

records.toxicity_detail: NC State Extension separately tags this species as a "Problem for Cats", "Problem for Dogs", and "Problem for Horses" (a distinct field from the same page's human-poisoning entry); the page gives no pet-specific symptom description beyond the tag itself.
records.name_note: RHS lists this species' "Name Status" as "Correct," and no admissible source proposes a different accepted binomial, so scientific_name_accepted is copied over unchanged from scientific_name_given.
unknowns: day_f_min/day_f_max/night_f_min/night_f_max: no source gives an ambient day/night temperature range for active growth — only USDA hardiness zones (3-9 per NC State/MOBOT/PSU) and an RHS H4 UK hardiness rating, which describe winter cold tolerance, not day/night care temperatures.

chill_damage_f: sources give only overall cold-hardiness zone ranges/ratings for the established, dormant plant (USDA 3-9; RHS H4 = hardy to -10 to -5°C), not an actionable frost/cold damage-onset temperature, so this was not mapped onto this field per the instruction against using a survival floor here.
humidity_need/humidity_pct_min/humidity_pct_max: not addressed by any admissible source for this outdoor garden perennial.

light_fc_min/light_fc_good/direct_sun_hours_max: sources give a sun-duration category (full sun = 6+ hrs/day, partial shade = 2-6 hrs/day per NC State) rather than a footcandle intensity value or an explicit upper bound on sun hours, so these numeric fields were left null; outdoor_sun_exposure captures the supported axis instead.

soil_ph_min/soil_ph_max: sources qualitatively disagree and give no numbers — Penn State Extension says soil should be 'neutral to alkaline' while RHS lists pH tolerance as 'Acid or Alkaline'; with no numeric range from either and a mismatch on whether acid soil is tolerated, this was left null rather than guessed.

water_regime (and its day-count/basis fields): NC State's own structured 'Soil Drainage' attribute lists 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry' as tolerated conditions, while its own prose and other sources (Clemson HGIC, University of Maryland Extension, Missouri Botanical Garden) stress a strict need for dry, well-drained soil and warn of root/crown rot if kept too wet — a genuine conflict between a source's structured tag and prose (and across sources), so left null rather than picking a side.

fertilize_interval_days/fertilize_strength/fertilize_active_months: no admissible source gives fertilizing guidance for this species; several instead emphasize it thrives in poor, low-fertility soil without describing any feeding schedule.

toxicity_detail is deliberately limited to the pet-specific 'Problem for Cats/Dogs/Horses' tag; NC State's fuller symptom/mechanism writeup on the same page sits under a separate 'Poisonous to Humans' heading and was not carried over, since it describes human, not pet, effects. RHS separately flags the species as generally 'Harmful if eaten' without naming an affected species, so it was not used to support toxic_to_pets either.

soil_drainage — removed on audit: soil_drainage is asserted as "fast" citing only Clemson HGIC's prose ("plant in a well-drained area, as root rot will become an issue if the soil is kept too wet"), but the record's own unknowns text — two fields later, for water_regime — discloses that NC State's own structured 'Soil Drainage' attribute for this exact species lists 'Good Drainage, Moist, Occasionally Dry' as tolerated conditions (confirmed live on plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/asclepias-tuberosa/, under Cultural Conditions). That is the same species-specific, admissible-source structured field directly on-topic for soil_drainage, and it names 'Moist' as a tolerated condition rather than a strict fast-draining-only requirement. The record treats this exact conflict as sufficient grounds to leave water_regime null, but never applies the same caution to soil_drainage — it picks 'fast' from a single source while sitting on, and not disclosing, a structured contradiction it had already identified for the closely related field.

normalizations: 2026-08-21: landed after one registry fix (garden-gnome commit 9afdde5), not a data fix. Black-Eyed Susan cited ask.ifas.ufl.edu/fp512 -- attributed in the researcher's own source string to the identical EDIS document edis.ifas.ufl.edu hosts -- which the loader correctly refused since the domain wasn't registered. Registered it alongside UF/IFAS's known domain, same authority, and the citations resolved cleanly on re-check.

All three species flagged in advance for toxicity attention -- Sweet Pea (a different genus from the already-landed edible garden pea, despite the name), Vinca (source of the vinca alkaloids), and Butterfly Weed (a milkweed, cardiac glycosides) -- correctly resolved toxic_to_pets=true. Sweet Pea and Vinca both kept toxicity_detail null rather than borrow their sources' human-toxicity writeups -- Sweet Pea's audit explicitly caught and stripped an embedded Lathyrism symptom list that had been copied from a 'Poisonous to Humans' section into the pet-facing field, the same anti-pattern found in b14 now generalizing correctly across unrelated species without being re-taught per batch. Scarlet Sage's record separately cross-checked its own common name against a real collision -- a different species (Salvia coccinea) shares the name 'scarlet sage' in some sources.
